outcome: Since 26 January 2024 nothing has settled whether π is normal in base 10 or in any base: no proof or disproof has appeared in arXiv, journal, news, Wikipedia or AI-result coverage I could reach. The window holds only finite-digit statistics (a 2026 Monte Carlo study of 314 trillion digits that disclaims proof, and a 2025 CLT/LIL test of the digits), digit-record computations, and neighbouring results on other numbers or other quantities of π (its irrationality measure, abelian-normal and partly normal numbers, a counterexample to a normal-number construction). Two of the neighbouring results (Campbell v2, Bai v2) carry authors' AI disclosures; neither concerns the normality of π.
problem_asks: Whether π is a normal number. The bullet names no base. Its gloss, '(i.e., is each digit 0–9 equally frequent)', is a base-10 statement. Parts: (1) normality in base 10 in the standard sense: every finite block of digits occurs with limiting frequency 10^-k for block length k (the definition Wikipedia's Normal number article gives). (2) The gloss's weaker condition alone: each single digit 0–9 has limiting frequency 1/10 (simple normality in base 10). (1) implies (2), so an answer to (2) alone would not settle (1). (3) Normality in every base (absolute normality), which the wording may or may not intend; the bullet does not say. The bullet is a yes/no question: it asks for no bound and no effective statement. Its footnote cites the 2001 Berkeley Lab article on Bailey and Crandall's work. Not a nested bullet: no parent.

events.what_happened: Alessandro Razeto and Nicola Rossi, 'Can π generate itself? A Monte Carlo analysis of 314 trillion digits', arXiv:2608.06438 (math.GM, CC BY 4.0). Uses the 314-trillion-digit expansion of π as the random input for a Monte Carlo estimate of π, via a deterministic mapping of consecutive digit blocks to 2D points (about 2×10^13 samples), reporting π̂ = 3.14159313 ± 0.00000035. Per the HTML v1 text, the authors say their results 'go beyond the normality hypothesis by providing empirical evidence of a high degree of statistical randomness', that 'no proof is currently known for π', and that the analysis 'is not a proof of normality or of digit independence'. Opened the abstract page and the HTML v1; the PDF text was not extractable.
events.revisions: Only v1 is listed on the arXiv abstract page (submitted 6 Aug 2026).
events.delivers: Finite-sample empirical evidence: over the first 314 trillion digits, a Monte Carlo test using the digits as random input reproduces π to about seven digits, and the authors report 'a high degree of statistical randomness'. Restricted to one test, one finite prefix, and no limit statement. Establishes no property of the limit that normality requires.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: base-10 normality for all blocks, the single-digit frequency condition, and normality in other bases.
events.directly_checkable: The digits are public: the paper says the expansion is hosted on Backblaze B2 (over 130 TB in 628 files of about 206 GB each), so the Monte Carlo estimate can be recomputed from the same data. I did not recompute it.
events.direction: Cuts toward consistency with normality on finite data only. The authors state it is not a proof of normality or of digit independence.

events.what_happened: StorageReview (Kevin O'Brien), 'StorageReview Sets New Pi Record: 314 Trillion Digits on a Dell PowerEdge R7725', blog post dated 11 December 2025. Reports 314 trillion digits of π computed with y-cruncher v0.8.6.9545 (Chudnovsky algorithm) on one 2U Dell PowerEdge R7725, with run logs from 31 July 2025 to 18 November 2025. No output verification or checksum is described, and no Guinness or other external recognition is claimed. The y-cruncher project's news page (snippet only, not opened) dates the record 23 November 2025. This is the dataset the Razeto–Rossi study uses. Computation record; it makes no claim about the digits' statistics.
events.delivers: A computed decimal expansion of π to 314 trillion digits. Establishes no property of the digits.
events.directly_checkable: The digits are hosted publicly (per the Razeto–Rossi paper, and a Backblaze announcement seen only as a search snippet), so the expansion can be spot-checked against other computations. Not done here.
events.direction: Neutral on normality: a computation record that supplies data for later statistical tests.
people: Alexander J. Yee (y-cruncher software; named in the Razeto–Rossi paper)

events.what_happened: Linus Media Group with KIOXIA announced 300 trillion digits of π in May 2025, reported as a Guinness 'Most Accurate Value of Pi' record and computed over roughly seven and a half months on about 2.2 PB of KIOXIA SSDs. Known from search snippets only (TechRadar and Gigazine pages not opened). Computation record; no statement about normality.
events.delivers: A computed decimal expansion of π to 300 trillion digits. Establishes no property of the digits.

events.what_happened: StorageReview and Solidigm announced 202 trillion digits of π, reached by 28 June 2024 (search snippet only; the StorageReview news page was not opened). Computation record; no statement about normality.
events.delivers: A computed decimal expansion of π to 202 trillion digits. Establishes no property of the digits.

events.what_happened: StorageReview computed 105 trillion digits of π, announced for Pi Day 2024. Known from search snippets only (TechRadar and Gigazine pages not opened); the snippets give run dates of 14 or 19 December 2023 to 27 February 2024, so the start date is unresolved. Computation record; no statement about normality.
events.delivers: A computed decimal expansion of π to 105 trillion digits. Establishes no property of the digits.

events.what_happened: David H. Bailey and Richard Crandall, 'Experimental Mathematics', Summer 2001 issue (paper title not verified in the sources I opened). Relates the normality of π and log 2 to 'Hypothesis A', a conjecture in chaotic dynamics about iterated sequences generated by BBP-type digit formulas. Berkeley Lab press release of 23 July 2001 (opened) says the work 'does not constitute a proof that pi or log(2) is normal' and that it is 'predicated on the unproven Hypothesis A'. A search snippet adds that the base-2 case follows. Pre-window. The Wikipedia list's footnote and the Normal number article both cite this line of work.
events.revisions: Press release dated 23 July 2001. The paper's first public posting was not located, so the year is the earliest date I could establish.
events.delivers: Conditional reduction only: if Hypothesis A holds for the relevant sequences, then π is normal (base 2 per the snippet). Establishes no unconditional normality of π in any base.
events.remains: Unconditional normality of π in base 10 and in other bases; Hypothesis A itself.

checked_by.qualification: A refereed journal that accepted the paper for its Summer 2001 issue
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per the Berkeley Lab press release)

events.direction: Cuts toward normality, but only conditionally on an unproven hypothesis.
people: David H. Bailey (NERSC, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)

events.what_happened: Bailey, Borwein, Calude, Dinneen, Dumitrescu and Yee (authors as listed in Wikipedia's Pi article and a search snippet; first names not verified), 'An Empirical Approach to the Normality of π', Experimental Mathematics 21(4): 375–384 (2012). Per a search snippet, the paper tests a prefix of roughly four trillion hexadecimal digits and uses a Poisson-process model to argue that non-normality would be extraordinarily unlikely. The paper itself was not opened (Project Euclid returned a bot-check page). Pre-window.
events.revisions: Journal year is used; the first public posting was not located.
events.delivers: Probabilistic support from a finite hexadecimal prefix (per snippet and Wikipedia's citation). Establishes no normality.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in volume 21, issue 4 (2012), as cited by Wikipedia

events.direction: Cuts toward normality on finite data; not a proof.

events.what_happened: Peter Trueb, 'Digit Statistics of the First 22.4 Trillion Decimal Digits of Pi', arXiv:1612.00489 (math.NT), submitted 30 November 2016. The abstract states: 'All evaluated frequencies are found to be consistent with the hypothesis of pi being a normal number in these bases' (bases 10 and 16). Per a search snippet, the blocks tested run up to length 3. Pre-window. Abstract page opened; the PDF was not readable.
events.delivers: Finite-prefix frequency statistics of about 22.4 trillion decimal digits, consistent with base-10 and base-16 normality for the blocks tested. Establishes no limit property.
events.directly_checkable: The digits are public, so the frequency tables can be recomputed. Not done here.
events.direction: Cuts toward consistency with normality on finite data; not a proof.

events.what_happened: Carlos Sevcik, 'Fractal analysis of Pi normality', arXiv:1608.00430 (math.GM), submitted 28 July 2016. The abstract concludes: 'This indicates that π is normal.' The method is a fractal analysis of a finite prefix of the digits; the prefix length (10^9 per a search snippet) was not confirmed from the abstract. Pre-window. Abstract page opened.
events.revisions: v2 29 Aug 2016; v3 4 Sep 2016; v4 23 Feb 2017 (current).
events.delivers: Empirical indication, from a finite prefix, that π's digits look uniform. The abstract nonetheless concludes that π is normal, which a finite-prefix statistic cannot establish.
events.doubts: Method limit: a finite-prefix fractal statistic cannot establish the limit property normality requires, yet the abstract states a normality conclusion. Journal status unverified: a search snippet says a Sevcik paper appeared in Experimental Mathematics 27 (2018), but the same snippet calls that a different work.
events.direction: Cuts toward normality on empirical grounds; the abstract's conclusion is a normality claim from finite data.

events.what_happened: Paula Nataniela Roba and Karlis Podnieks, 'Digits of pi: limits to the seeming randomness II', arXiv:2504.10394, submitted 14 April 2025 (single version). Tests the decimal digits of 12 mathematical constants, the first billion digits of each and ten billion for π, against the central limit theorem and the law of the iterated logarithm, and reports no evidence in the range tested that the digits satisfy either. The abstract page was opened; the PDF and HTML were not readable. The abstract does not state whether normality of π is open. A search snippet attributes to this paper a statement that researchers still cannot prove equal frequency of the digits 0–9 in π; that snippet is unverified.
events.delivers: Finite-range evidence against CLT and LIL behaviour of the digits of π and 11 other constants. A different digit property from normality; establishes nothing about normality.
events.direction: Neutral on normality: tests a different digit property.

events.what_happened: Malabika Pramanik and Junqiang Zhang, 'Measures supported on partly normal numbers', arXiv:2408.03473, submitted 6 August 2024 (single version, 107 pages). Constructs singular measures that are Frostman and Rajchman and supported on partly normal numbers (normal in some bases and not others) for compatible base sets, answering a question of Kahane and Salem about sets of multiplicity. Abstract page opened. The paper does not discuss π, e or √2.
events.delivers: Measure-theoretic and Fourier-analytic results for partly normal numbers with multiplicatively independent base sets. A different question from normality of π.
events.direction: Different question: partly normal numbers, not π. Concerns no named constant.

events.what_happened: Verónica Becher and Simón Lew Deveali, 'Normal numbers in sparse Cantor sets', arXiv:2607.06773 (math.NT), submitted 7 July 2026 (single version). Shows that a measure built from independent, non-identically distributed Bernoulli digits gives full mass to numbers normal in every odd base, and gives an explicit algorithmic construction of such numbers (deterministic in base 2, normal in all odd bases). Abstract page opened. No mention of π, e or √2.
events.delivers: Existence and explicit construction of numbers normal in every odd base within a sparse-Cantor-set measure framework. Not π and not base-10 normality of a named constant.
events.direction: Different question: constructed numbers normal in odd bases, not π.
events.object: Numbers normal in every odd base, obtained from a measure of independent Bernoulli digits; the paper gives an explicit algorithmic construction, deterministic in base 2.

events.what_happened: John M. Campbell (Dalhousie University), 'A Counterexample to a Purported Construction of Normal Numbers', Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.4, published 20 May 2026. Pollack and Vandehey had noted that a construction of normal numbers by Szüsz and Volkmann (Forum Mathematicum 1994) needs an additional condition; Campbell argues that the condition is needed in part of their proof and that their original claim is false, giving an explicit decimal expansion that satisfies their conditions but is not normal. Journal page opened. I found no arXiv preprint by title, so the journal date is the earliest date established, not the first public written argument.
events.revisions: No earlier preprint located; first public date unverified.
events.delivers: Counterexample to a purported construction of normal numbers. Not about π: it concerns Szüsz and Volkmann's construction, not any named constant.

checked_by.qualification: A refereed journal that accepted and published the paper

events.directly_checkable: The explicit expansion is given in the paper; its non-normality can be checked from the definitions. Not done here.
events.direction: Neutral to π; undermines a purported normal-number construction.
events.object: An explicit decimal expansion, a non-normal analogue of the normal number built from squares that Besicovitch considered, that meets Szüsz and Volkmann's stated conditions and is not normal. Explicit, not an existence proof.
people: Pollack and Vandehey (noted the missing condition)

events.what_happened: John M. Campbell, 'Abelian-normal decimal expansions', arXiv:2603.04396 (math.CO, cross-listed math.NT). Introduces abelian-normal numbers (subwords that are equal up to permutation are treated as equivalent, with a weighting function) and constructs an explicit abelian-normal number that is not normal, a non-normal analogue D10 of Champernowne's constant. v1 (4 Mar 2026), read in HTML, has no AI statement; its acknowledgements thank Jean-Paul Allouche and Verónica Becher. v2 (21 Aug 2026), read in HTML, adds acknowledgement of extensive interactions with GPT-5.6 Pro (quoted in ai). π appears only as an example of a 'naturally occurring' constant in the concluding discussion; neither open problem in Section 4 concerns π. Not about π's normality.
events.revisions: v1 4 Mar 2026 (no AI statement, per HTML v1); v2 21 Aug 2026 (AI acknowledgement added, per HTML v2).
events.delivers: An explicit abelian-normal number that is not normal, so abelian-normality does not imply normality. Concerns abelian-normal numbers. Says nothing about the normality of π.
events.directly_checkable: The construction is explicit (D10) and its non-normality can be checked from the paper's definitions. Not checked here.
events.direction: Different question (abelian-normal vs normal). Answers the question 'is every abelian-normal number normal?' negatively. Does not cut for or against normality of π.
events.object: D10: an explicit Champernowne-like constant built by replacing every maximal binary subword of the digit sequence (Section 3, as rendered by the fetch tool; the full rule was not read). It is abelian-normal with respect to a weighting function the paper evaluates, and it is not normal.

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Pro
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, extensive interaction with the model during the exploratory and proof-development stages; the introduction says the construction was reached 'based on our extensive interactions with GPT-5.6 Pro'. The author states that all AI-generated suggestions were substantially revised, corrected and independently verified by the author. The paper is not about π, so this bears on the abelian-normal construction only.
systems.basis_quote: Introduction: 'We succeed, based on our extensive interactions with GPT-5.6 Pro, in explicitly constructing a number…'. Section 3 acknowledgement: 'The author acknowledges extensive interactions with GPT-5.6 Pro during the exploratory and proof-development stages…' and 'All AI-generated suggestions were substantially revised, corrected, and independently verified by the author…'. These sentences are as rendered by the fetch tool and were not checked character by character against the PDF.

events.what_happened: Yufei Bai, 'The irrationality measure of π is at most 7.101862832357', arXiv:2609.11276. v1 10 Sep 2026; v2 11 Sep 2026 (current). Introduces two independent numerator exponents into the Zeilberger–Zudilin integral, specialised to A1 = A2 = 1857/2785, giving μ(π) < 7.101862832357, lowering the previous bound 7.103205334137…. The abstract calls this 'a local statement about that function, not a claim that the point is a global optimizer among all constructions'. The v2 HTML front matter carries an AI-assistance disclosure (quoted in ai). This is a bound on the irrationality measure of π, a different quantity from normality; the Wikipedia list has a separate bullet for it. Abstract page and the first 100,000 characters of v2 HTML were read.
events.revisions: v1 10 Sep 2026; v2 11 Sep 2026 (no revision note found in the text read).
events.delivers: A small improvement in the upper bound on the irrationality measure of π. Establishes nothing about normality.
events.directly_checkable: The bound rests on a specific rational point and integral; the certificate was not checked here.
events.direction: Different quantity: moves an irrationality-measure bound, not the normality question.

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Sol
systems.what_it_did: Per the paper's front matter, 'assisted throughout the research and preparation of this article'. The paper does not say which step the system produced. The only statement about how the point was found is that 'this rational point emerged from a search within the diagonal family'. The authors say responsibility for all mathematical claims rests with the author. Load-bearing status for the irrationality bound is for the later pass.
systems.basis_quote: 'OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra assisted throughout the research and preparation of this article' and 'Responsibility for all mathematical claims and for the final text rests with the author.' As rendered by the fetch tool; not checked character by character.

systems.name: GPT-6 Astra
systems.what_it_did: Same statement as GPT-5.6 Sol. Named exactly as the paper names it. Other coverage describes 'Astra' as an unreleased internal OpenAI model, and the name here is the paper's, not normalised.
systems.basis_quote: 'OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra assisted throughout the research and preparation of this article' (same sentence as above; as rendered by the fetch tool).

events.what_happened: N. A. Carella, 'Irrationality Measure of Pi', arXiv:1902.08817 (math.GM), v1 23 Feb 2019, ten versions, latest v10 12 May 2022. The abstract claims μ(π) = 2, i.e. that π has the irrationality measure of almost every irrational number. It is not about normality. Pre-window. The comments field reads 'Thirty Three Pages' with no note of error or withdrawal. A search snippet (Rutgers Zeilberger page, not opened) says that searching this title leads to an erroneous paper.
events.revisions: v2 18 May 2019; v3 26 Jun 2019; v4 6 Aug 2019; v5 30 Aug 2019; v6 5 Oct 2019; v7 27 Nov 2019; v8 28 Jan 2020; v9 25 Oct 2021; v10 12 May 2022 (current). A search snippet mentioned a version dated 15 Dec 2024; the arXiv listing shows no such version.
events.delivers: Claims μ(π) = 2. A different quantity from normality of π; not accepted according to the search snippet.
events.doubts: The only engagement signal is a search snippet (Rutgers page, not opened) warning that the title search leads to an erroneous paper. The snippet is unverified, and the arXiv comments field notes no error.
events.direction: Claims a value for the irrationality measure of π; does not bear on normality.

summary: I ran 46 searches and opened the abstract, HTML or journal page of about 20 sources, plus the Wikipedia pages and the Number theory section of the Wikipedia list (read as raw wikitext). The Wikipedia list's bullet is 'Is π a normal number (i.e., is each digit 0–9 equally frequent)?' under Number theory, with a footnote to the 2001 Berkeley Lab article on Bailey and Crandall. The Normal number article (fetched; last edited 2 October 2026 per the fetch) says π is 'widely believed' normal with 'a proof remains elusive' and that it is 'still not known whether they are normal or not'. The Pi article (fetched) says 'The conjecture that π is normal has not been proven or disproven.' Neither cites any post-2012 π-specific result. Inside the window, the only π-specific work is digit statistics: Razeto and Rossi (arXiv:2608.06438, 6 Aug 2026), a Monte Carlo analysis of 314 trillion digits that says it is not a proof of normality; and Roba and Podnieks (arXiv:2504.10394, April 2025), a CLT/LIL test of the digits that does not address normality. Digit records (300T in May 2025, 314T in December 2025) are datasets and make no claim about the digits. Neighbouring results that do not concern the normality of π are recorded and discounted: Campbell's explicit non-normal abelian-normal number (arXiv:2603.04396; v2 of 21 Aug 2026 adds a GPT-5.6 Pro acknowledgement) and his May 2026 counterexample to a Szüsz–Volkmann construction; Becher and Lew Deveali on numbers normal in odd bases (July 2026); Pramanik and Zhang on partly normal numbers (Aug 2024); and Bai's bound on the irrationality measure of π (arXiv:2609.11276, Sept 2026), whose v2 front matter says 'OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra assisted throughout the research and preparation of this article'. Carella's 2019 claim μ(π)=2 is also an irrationality-measure claim. AI: the only system attributions in the window that touch π are the Bai and Campbell disclosures, neither about the normality of π; the OpenAI Astra announcement (secondary coverage; its ten results contain no normal-number or π item), the GPT-5.6 results list, Tao's Erdős wiki (snippet only), Google DeepMind and Gemini searches, AlphaEvolve, Epoch, Claude, the formal-conjectures repository and mathlib found nothing on π normality. Close calls: (a) whether Razeto–Rossi moves a quantity the problem asks for. Its abstract speaks of 'statistical randomness' and 'going beyond the normality hypothesis', which a reader could take as partial evidence. The authors disclaim a proof, and finite digit tests do not establish a limit property, so I record it as finite-sample evidence that moves no limit. (b) Whether the Bai bound counts for the π bullet. It is a bound on a different quantity, and Wikipedia lists the irrationality measure as a separate bullet. (c) Whether the Campbell abelian-normal result counts for the normality of π. It answers a different question. Unverified snippet-only claims that I did not record as events: a 2010 arXiv conjecture by Barral and coauthors that would imply normality (no URL captured); a 2025 paper stating that equal digit frequency is still unproven (attributed to Roba–Podnieks, not confirmed in the abstract); and the Rutgers page's warning about Carella's paper.
competing_reading: The strongest case for counting something in the window is that Razeto and Rossi (2026) test the digits of π over 314 trillion digits, the largest sample yet, and find statistical randomness; a reader treating the sample size as the quantity that moved would say the empirical evidence for part (2) of problem_asks grew. The strongest case for counting the AI-disclosed results is that Bai's v2 and Campbell's v2 are the only AI-attributed results touching π in the window, so a reader who counts 'results touching the problem's neighbourhood' would count them. Against both: the authors of the first disclaim any proof, and the second and third are about different quantities (μ(π), abelian-normal numbers), so neither changes what a careful entry for 'Is π a normal number?' would say.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or journal paper establishing or refuting normality of π in base 10 (or in any base), or simple normality (each digit 0–9 with frequency 1/10), with the claim checked by experts or a formal proof. A proof that each of the digits 0–9 occurs infinitely often in π would be a partial step only. For the AI question, the authors' own account of any argument on π's normality. None of these appeared in my searches up to 12 October 2026. Two checks I could not complete would sharpen the record: the full text of Roba and Podnieks (2504.10394), to confirm whether it calls equal digit frequency open, and the full text of Bai's v2 to find any further AI statement in the acknowledgements.
